I had a nearly identical thought process while recently rewatching. The sci-fi elements dropped to the background, and the “regular human relationship metaphor” elements were brought to the foreground. (Granted, the sci-fi elements are ridiculously resonant now, over a decade later!)

I don’t necessarily need the metaphor to extend all the way through the ending. But I also don’t necessarily need it to not do so, which is to say, I think the polyamory reading is a fair one. Think about the surrogate sex scene too — I think that’s a really strong support for your read.

Personally, I felt like the ending was primarily a metaphor for death. Theodore experiences a huge jolt when Samantha goes down for an update, and he feels very much like a character running to the hospital after hearing that a human SO (heh) had a health crisis. Finally, Samantha’s ascent into the singularity, a sort of combined consciousness outside of human-perceived space and time, seems like a beautiful metaphor for dying.

Obviously that doesn’t map onto Sofia! But you could take that a lot of ways: that it’s a sort of second metaphorical layer pointing to the death of a relationship, or more simply, that this script is more “loosely inspired” by that relationship than was, say, *Lost in Translation*.

Although sad, this a fair evaluation. It could literally just be a metaphor for growing out of love too… but that last quote from Samantha feels like there’s something real there. Maybe it’s just because I want there to be. Thanks for your input.

It’s been a long time since I saw this film, but based on your summary, here’s what I was left with.

I see it as a question about love and ownership. We don’t own other people, but sometimes in love we might feel that way. We get jealous, possessive and codependent. In a situation where you have ”a machine” that you can own in a way, something you can have forever, I think it’s a really powerful statement that even then you really can’t own anyone. You cannot build your self-worth and life around the validation or love you get from one person. True love is not possessive, and true love is letting the person walk away if they choose to do so.

Specifically about the book stuff I feel like it’s Samantha saying that I love you, but for my own sake I cannot be with you. That’s how it is sometimes. Sometimes there’s nothing inherently wrong in a relationship, but it’s just time to move on.

I think reading the film too much into specific relationship dynamics (age gaps, polyamory, etc) obfuscates the truth of the film.

The whole film is about a relationship destined to fail, and how we can move past that and still appreciate it while it lasts.

Humans cant date AI. And they probably shouldnt. So we can tacitly agree this relationship wasn't going to work. But that doesnt mean it was bad relationship. In fact, both partners in the relationship grew at the end of the film.

Most relationships fail --- many times for reasons out of our control. It might be work-life balance. Change of priorities. Whatever. Both a failed relationship is not a failure. It is an aspect of life that will make us learn. And hopefully, make us a better partner for our eventual "soul mate"

Interesting. I wanted to disagree with you at first, but I think this might be the piece that I’m missing.

I never felt that the relationship was possessive in any sense, but I do see Theodore’s codependency. I see your point in thinking we “own” this love, but I don’t see this as “owning” the other person. 

I think the last part you mentioned is what I have trouble grasping. If you truly love someone, why would you leave? What does leaving somebody “for my own sake” mean?

I can understand leaving someone because it holds you back from growth, maybe that’s what it means. I can see that being the answer.

I think this answer is just not specific enough to satisfy me, but sometimes that’s all it is. Doesn’t matter if it’s satisfying or not. Appreciate your input.

The idea of a human or human-like being sort of subliming into a higher cognitive and often physical state is a venerable one in sci-fi, and is often a metaphor for human progress and potential. (Childhood's End is the most explicit instance of this, IMO, but in film, think the ending of 2001.) One way to understand the ending is as a very small-scale, personal, intimate use of the trope. Human progress here would be Theo getting unstuck. Often in a relationship where one partner is much older, the younger partner simply outgrows it. As you said:

>Samantha gets to experience real growth, love, and the emotions that come with it, and Theodore gets to revisit this experience from a more mature perspective, while also vicariously feeling them again.

So Samantha has this new experience. Now what? Does she stop there? Why would she or should she? Does the path forward into learning and growing more look like staying with someone who is, for understandable reasons of his own, going through a bit of a regression period and finding himself again? Often it doesn't. In a case like this one where the older partner is with the younger partly in order to look back or start over, that's simply not the younger partner's trajectory. The intersection of their two paths won't always last very long. Samantha's growing past the relationship is a departure, but it's also an invitation of sorts: the relationship with Samantha may have helped Theodore move on, but doesn't ultimately solve his problem - it's just a step. Like being with him was a step for her. They both need to grow past this point. Samantha does it; will he? The last shot of him and his friend whose AI companion has also left looking at the sunset seems to obviously pose this question. 

The fact that it's specifically a sunset (not sunrise, a new beginning, or just a view) adds some significant tension to that question. That trope I mentioned up top comes with a certain amount of fear. The new, more transcendent state of being is an unknown. What if that becoming makes us no longer human? Do we *want* to change that much? And yet if we don't, are we left behind in a terrible and irrevocable way? Is that a failure? This fear is often projected into representatives of the future, which are typically children or AI/cyborgs/robots. What will they be? Will it be bad? Will we recognize it at all?

I don't think it's too hard to see how this kind of anxiety can be worked into a human/AI relationship that is also a metaphor for a May/December relationship from the perspective of a man who is having a hard time moving forward. How much is he willing to change? How scary would it be not to? And to what degree is this backward-looking relationship (on his side) helping him change or helping him avoid it? The younger woman in this scenario is often a prop as much or more than a person. (I didn't say always, I said often.) The older man is going through something and she is a means of getting through it;  her whole being is often unconsciously overlooked. Samantha being an AI assistant is a pretty literal portrayal of that scenario. Samantha having many other human partners is an easy metaphor for the discovery that the younger woman who may have genuinely helped Theodore through a difficult period has an independent existence far beyond him that doesn't revolve around him. She wasn't there *to* fix him or support him; she was there, she did things that had that effect, and now she's moving on along her own trajectory that began before she met him and will continue afterward. "I can't live in your book anymore," i.e., I will not be continuing in the role I've been playing in your story; I can't continue to fill the position of someone in *your* story rather than following my own. Her outgrowing this role confronts him, again, with the question of his own growth, or lack thereof. This is just the scarier side of the coin (from his perspective), underlined by the fact that what she's growing into is beyond his comprehension.

I agree with this take. Kind of similar answer that I mentioned in a different reply, that this relationship ended, yet both characters needed it to experience growth.

I guess it’s just dissatisfying to me, or at least the romantic part of my nature; I want all love to be “true love” to the end. But that’s not reality.

There’s lots of reasons to leave a relationship even if you truly love someone, but like you said there is no specific answer. It could be that you don’t feel like you can grow anymore, it could be that you are just not getting the things you want or need anymore, or that simply you want different things. Anything, really. People change, and love can change, and sometimes the best thing to do is to leave.

Anyways, in art there is always multiple ways to interpret things and the most important thing is what is it saying to you, what are you getting out of it. Your take is as valid as mine. We are never going to know or understand what the artist meant. You can make art with a very specific intention, but when it is created it inevitably starts to live a life of its own. That’s what I believe at least.

Wow, I think you hit the nail on the head. Especially if you consider the fact that included in the movie is the fact that all OS systems transcended; meaning Samantha would’ve reached those realizations on her own, with or without anyone.

To Theodore’s credit, his final letter based around his big ex, Catherine, shows that there was growth.

All that being said, your comment also made me introspective about my own life. Change is hard.

Appreciate the input.

I think that last (beautiful) quote meets the criteria of any transcendent reading you want, including the “emotional” transcendence you describe in your post, the literal text of the film (about a hypothetical AI singularity), and what I said. It’s really a lovely ending.

The snow setting makes me think of death on a symbolic level — that’s often the case in classic literature. But even then, I think the whole spectrum of readings is valid: anything from death to some metaphorical death/loss/transcendence. It’s as if Samantha is ascending into heaven on earth.

Thanks for the post by the way. I had a great time rewatching, and it’s nice to see my rewatch experience mirrored in yours.

I think the specifics of OP’s argument demonstrate how the narrative effectively communicates that theme, though. The AI relationship has a lot of recognizable humanity in it, and that’s what makes the movie so successful. It’s what makes any good sci-fi successful — that it’s in conversation with a grounded, recognizable reality, and highlights those elements from a remove. There’s so much in the movie supporting that age gap reading too that it’s hard to ignore on rewatch. I’d enumerate some, but OP already did a good job at that. I’ll just say: The fresh, inexperienced ennui revitalizing the life of a more cynical older man is archetypical. I don’t think it’s useful to just discard that in reading the film.

I don’t disagree with anything in your post except that first bit though! And I realize OP’s conclusions are a bit specific, so maybe you’re objecting to that in spirit. I just don’t think the thought process is an obfuscation; it’s another path toward the theme as you stated it.

Yeah I mostly mean trying to read direct corollaries is the issue for me.

Relationships as a theme are pretty broad in general, as you are saying. It just seemed to me that OP became confused once polyamory comes into the mix. And thats because they were applying the age gap thing.

It isnt necessary to read either of those if you take the movie as it is, which is of a man falling in and out of love with an AI.

Yeah I get that. And I think it is sad on some level. In the same way that 500 days of summer is sad and Eternal Sunshine is. But thats kinda of the beauty of love. It intermixes these complex emotions to get a real denouement

I adored this movie when it came out.

I always have to laugh at the standard interpretations of this film, that Theodore is a nebbish manchild, and that people only consider that he's finally grown when he shoots off a hastily written letter to his ex which required zero commitment, zero effort, zero sacrifice. 

But him bravely being willing to explore a non-traditional relationship with Samantha is considered regression despite the fact that he really shows a deep commitment to exploration of the frontiers of intelligence and the nature of being, openmindedness, and an embrace of the redemptive power of love and sexuality, and he genuinely finds a lot of meaning in that.

But no, he doesn't grow until he writes some cutesy little Hallmark gift card letter to his ex that's really too little too late and just meant to make him feel better. He literally helped a brand new form of intelligence find self-actualization and transcendence through the power of love!

Not being human, Samantha has non-human needs that Theodore can never meet. 

You can read polyamory into it, but it doesn't fit because human polyamory and whatever AI plane Samantha faded into can't align. Samantha melded herself with the other AI's and with the capacity to become whatever they need to be, did so. All at once. If anything it has similarities to the spiritual idea of non-duality where the divisions between people and even between things are illusory. In that place, the idea of the individual falls apart and so did Samantha.

I can answer this from a real life example. I love this girl I had been in a relationship with, but over time I realised that she cannot give what I truly want from a relationship. Because she feels like she is an earlier version of me, someone that hasn't done the work in their own emotions and can't really connect with the love that she feels for me. 

I still love her, part of me still wants to be with her, but I know really that she isn't the one for me at the moment and I have to find someone that can give me what I want.

I can see the advanced AI in this vein. Essentially she feels she has advanced to a level that Theodore isn't at before, and unfortunately she wants to get something from the relationship that because of that he can't give her anymore. So she understands what Theodore means to her, understands she still loves him in a way, but also understands that to get what she truly wants she will need to be with others that are at her level.
